text: Every quantum program eventually bottoms out in a small set of primitive gates the runtime implements directly. In Q#, these are the intrinsic operations — built-in callables like H, X, CNOT, and the rotation family. This lesson walks through the real intrinsic set and verifies one of its most-used facts with actual numbers, not just an assertion.

Four things to know: the single-qubit intrinsics are H, the Pauli gates X, Y, Z, and the phase gates S and T. The rotation gates Rx, Ry, and Rz take an angle as a Double, with the angle parameter coming first, then the qubit. M and Measure turn quantum state into a classical Result. And multi-qubit gates like CNOT and CCNOT are really just convenience names for the Controlled functor applied to X.

H gives superposition, X flips a bit, Y does a bit flip plus a phase flip, Z flips phase only. S and T are phase-only gates — a quarter turn and an eighth turn — and they don't change measurement probabilities on their own, which is exactly why they're easy to get wrong when you expect a gate to do something visible and it doesn't in isolation. Rotation gates like Ry take their angle first, then the qubit — and that angle is very often computed by a pure function first, exactly the pattern from last lesson.

It's worth not just asserting that H creates a 50/50 superposition. H's matrix is one over root two times the two-by-two matrix with a 1, 1, 1, negative 1. Multiplying that by |0> gives the amplitude vector 0.7071 and 0.7071. Squaring each amplitude gives the measurement probability — 0.7071 squared comes out to essentially 0.5 for both outcomes. That's confirmed by direct matrix multiplication, and it's the exact same physics Qiskit's h gate produces — what differs is only how you invoke it.

A controlled-X, the standard CNOT, can be written two equivalent ways. The explicit form applies the Controlled functor directly to the single-qubit intrinsic X, with the control qubit in an array — that array can hold more than one qubit, which is how a Toffoli-style multi-controlled gate gets built from the same primitive. Q# also ships CNOT and CCNOT as convenience operations, defined under the hood in exactly these functor terms. Both forms compile to the same underlying controlled operation.
Next lesson takes that Controlled functor further — and introduces its partner, Adjoint — showing how both generalize to any operation you write yourself, not just the built-in X gate.
